newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia banks seen within property exposure limits.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia banks seen within property exposure limits.

text.p: Most Malaysian banks have not exceeded exposure limits imposed by Bank Negara last month on lending to buy property or shares, analysts said on Wednesday.
They said banks that had submitted their loan outstandings in the two sectors to Bank Negara by the Tuesday deadline were generally within the central bank's guidelines.

"Almost all the banks we contacted said they were within Bank Negara's guidelines on property lending and everyone said they were below the limits on share financing," said a banking analyst at a foreign brokerage house in Kuala Lumpur.
"Assuming they were telling the truth," he added
On March 28, Malaysia's central bank said commercial banks could lend only up to 20 percent of their overall outstanding loans for property purchases and 15 percent for financing share purchases.
Banks exceeding the limits were asked to submit compliance plans by April 15, and quarterly reports thereafter, on how they were reducing their overall exposure.

Even though some banks had exceeded the limits on property financing, a large part of their portfolios was invested in infrastructure-related projects and would therefore not be counted, said a dealer at a local stockbroking house.

For example, Malayan Banking Bhd (Maybank) had lent 27 percent of its total loans to the property sector, with 15 percent going to infrastructure-related projects and only 12 percent going to property purchases, said the dealer.
The next step for the banks would be to reduce their exposures to the sectors over time, Bank Negara said in its April 8 statement.

Arab Malaysian Merchant Bank had lent out 27.1 percent, Public Bank Bhd 35 percent, DCB Bank Bhd 27 percent, and Kwong Yik Bank Bhd 24 percent of their total outstandings to the property sector, said the dealer.
All these banks' exposures included lending for infrastructure projects, but they had not broken down the figures to show the proportion of infrastructure lending.

Banks that had submitted their share financing exposures were Arab Malaysian Merchant Bank at 17 percent, Public Bank at 18 percent, DCB Bank at 20 percent and Kwong Yik Bank at 21 percent, said the dealer.
These figures included lending for financing business ventures, bringing the actual proportion of their exposure to share financing below the stipulated limit, he said.
Analysts said among banks that may have to slow down lending to these sectors were Multi Purpose Bank Bhd, Pacific Bank Bhd, Hong Leong Bank Bhd, Allied Bank (Malaysia) Bhd, MBf Capital Bhd and AMMB.
Officials at all the banks mentioned were not available for comment.

On Tuesday, Bank Negara clarified its lending restrictions, banking sources said. The restrictions would include working capital requirements for stockbroking firms, but would exclude profit guarantees by merchant banks for companies seeking stock exchange listing, banking sources said.
The central bank made it clear earlier in the month that any restrictions it imposed would have some flexibility and would be implemented over time.
Some banks had yet to submit their exposures to property and share financing, said a Bank Negara spokesman. "But we have to be flexible, and allow them time to compile their figures," he said.
